summary: Extends RSVP Graceful Restart for GMPLS so a restarting node can recover its signaling state from the Path message it last sent. Earlier mechanisms recovered state from neighbors when the data plane kept working. This extension covers more of the cases where a node restarts. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If a worker forgets what job they were on after a reboot, they can look at the last note they wrote down and carry on. This lets restarting routers do something similar.

questions: how do routers recover rsvp state after restart
what is the rsvp capability object
subtitle: How a restarting GMPLS router gets back the RSVP Path state it lost, by asking its downstream neighbors to play it back.

tldr.problem: Earlier RSVP Graceful Restart could not fully recover signaling state on an ingress node, or every RSVP object such as the Explicit Route Object, because the data plane does not hold all of it.
tldr.mechanism: A downstream neighbor sends the restarting node a new RecoveryPath message, a copy of the last Path message it received from that node. Hello messages carry a new Capability object to negotiate this, and Summary Refresh can select which LSPs to recover.
tldr.outcome: The restarting node can rebuild all previously sent Path state and match it to the forwarding state that survived. The extensions never create or restore data plane state.

facts.label: Capability flags
facts.value: T, R and S, one bit each

today: RFC 5063 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007. It updates RFC 2961 and RFC 3473, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Graceful Restart Could Not Recover
sections.content:
RSVP Graceful Restart, defined in RFC 3473 and built on the Hello mechanism of RFC 3209, lets an RSVP agent resynchronize after a restart when the data plane kept its forwarding state. The restarting node learns what it lost from updates sent by its neighbors.

This RFC addresses two gaps. First, the data plane alone does not hold enough to rebuild every previously sent Path message. The text gives the Protection, Admin Status, Session Attribute, Notify Request and Sender Tspec objects as examples, along with the Explicit Route Object (ERO). A transit node may also have modified the Path state it received, and that cannot be rebuilt internally. Second, an ingress node that does not preserve full RSVP state across restarts had no good way to recover.

The extensions only rebuild control plane state that matches forwarding state already in place. They are not used to create or restore data plane state.
sections.eli5: After a reboot, a router forgets some of the notes it had written about each connection. The old rules could not always give those notes back, so this adds a way to get them back.

sections.title: The RecoveryPath Message
sections.content:
The new RecoveryPath message has the same format as a Path message but uses a new message number, 30, so it can be told apart. Its IP destination address MUST be the same as the destination of the Resv message last generated by the sender.

It carries the contents of the last Path message the downstream neighbor received from the restarting node. Some objects are not copied as they were: the MESSAGE_ID, MESSAGE_ID_ACK and MESSAGE_ID_NACK objects and the Integrity object are generated fresh under the rules of RFC 2961 and RFC 2747. The RSVP Hop object is copied from the most recent Resv message sent to the restarted node, and a Recovery Label object MUST be added with the label value taken from the latest Resv message's Label object.
sections.eli5: The neighbor writes out a copy of the last note it got from the restarted router, with a couple of lines changed so it fits the situation, and hands it back.

sections.title: Negotiating with the Capability Object
sections.content:
Neighbors discover support through a new Capability object in RSVP Hello messages. It uses Class-Number 134 and C-Type 1, and has three flag bits:

  • T (RecoveryPath Transmit Enabled): the sender can send RecoveryPath messages.
  • R (RecoveryPath Desired): the sender wants to receive them.
  • S (RecoveryPath Srefresh Capable): with R set, the sender can handle Srefresh messages carrying the RecoveryPath flag.

Reserved bits MUST be zero on send and ignored on receipt, and an absent object is treated as all bits cleared. Nodes supporting the extension MUST be able to set both T and R, and SHOULD set both by default.

A restarting node that wants this recovery sets R and also includes the Restart_Cap object from RFC 3473. If either side lacks support, the restarting node and its neighbor fall back to the plain RFC 3473 procedures. A node that does not know the object discards it, because its Class-Number has the form 10bbbbbb.
sections.eli5: Before anyone helps, the two routers hold up signs saying 'I can help' or 'please help me'. If the signs do not match, they use the old way.

sections.title: Recovery Procedures
sections.content:
A downstream neighbor that sees a capable restarting node MUST send a RecoveryPath message for each LSP for which it has sent a Resv message. It SHOULD do so within about half of the advertised Recovery Time, spread out so the restarted CPU is not overloaded. It SHOULD resend until it gets a Message ID acknowledgment or a Path message for that LSP; without Message IDs, at least 3 attempts should fit before 3/4 of the Recovery Time has passed.

The restarting node matches each RecoveryPath message, and for non-ingress LSPs the Path message with a Recovery Label, to forwarding state. The upstream interface and label come from the Path message, and the downstream interface and label from the RecoveryPath message. If complete forwarding state is found, the LSP is treated as resynchronized and the node MUST send a trigger Path message downstream, with an ERO that SHOULD match the one received. If no forwarding state is found, the Path message is treated as a new LSP setup, and the information from downstream is only advisory.

At the end of the Recovery Period, state installed from a RecoveryPath message that was not resynchronized SHOULD be discarded.
sections.eli5: The neighbor reads back each old note, and the restarted router checks it against what it can still see on the road. If it all matches, it carries on. Notes that do not match get thrown away at the end.

sections.title: Selective Recovery with Summary Refresh
sections.content:
If the restarting node has already recovered some LSPs locally, it does not need RecoveryPath messages for those. RecoveryPath Summary Refresh extends the Summary Refresh of RFC 2961 to let it pick. When a node sets both R and S in its Hello messages, its neighbor sends Srefresh messages whose MESSAGE_ID LIST objects have the new RecoveryPath Flag, 0x02, set. They list Message Identifiers of received Path state that has not been updated since the restart.

The restarted node matches each identifier against the Path messages it sent before the restart. A match counts as if a RecoveryPath message had been received, and it MUST generate a trigger Path message. With no match it MUST send a MESSAGE_ID NACK, also with the RecoveryPath Flag set, and the neighbor then generates a RecoveryPath message for that state. The neighbor MAY spread its Srefresh messages across 1/4 of the Recovery Time.
sections.eli5: Instead of reading back every note, the neighbor reads out just the note numbers. The restarted router only asks for the ones it does not remember.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it adds no new security considerations beyond those of existing RSVP hop-by-hop messages and Hello objects. The new message is limited to one RSVP hop. Cryptographic protection from RFC 2747 can be used with it.

The procedures assume full trust between RSVP neighbors: nothing verifies that restart information maps correctly to what was exchanged before. The recovery also adds processing for neighbors, which a restarting node can ease by using a large enough Recovery Time. A restarting node MUST NOT create or change forwarding state to match a RecoveryPath message that does not fit, and SHOULD log or report such an event because it might be an attack.
sections.eli5: The routers have to trust each other. A restarted router also must not simply believe a note that does not match what it sees, and it should tell someone about it.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA is asked to register the Capability object with Class-Number 134 and the RecoveryPath message with RSVP message type 30. The RFC also creates a new 32-bit-wide name space in the Capability object, with new registrations by IETF Consensus. The bits defined so far are T, R and S, one bit each.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers gets two new entries so that no one else uses the same numbers.
